title: Advanced Para Jumbles — 6 Sentences
tagline: Year 3 — Ordering six jumbled sentences using openers, links, chronology, pronouns and closers

introduction.overview: In a para-jumble question, six sentences from one paragraph are shuffled and you must restore the order. The method is to look for one opener (a sentence that does not depend on any other), one closer (a sentence that sums up or concludes), and then chains of links between the rest: pronouns that need antecedents, time words, "also" and "however" connectors, and cause-effect pairs.
introduction.placementRelevance: Six-sentence jumbles are the harder form of the standard ordering item and appear in verbal sections of company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Putting a set of notes or an email thread into a logical sequence uses the same cues.

learningObjectives: Find the opener and the closer
Use pronoun and article cues (a/the, it/they)
Build mini-chains and then join them
Eliminate options by the first two sentences

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A new idea is introduced with "a/an" and refers back with "the"; pronouns need something to refer to.

coreDefinitions: Opener: a sentence that introduces the topic without referring back.
Closer: a sentence that concludes, summarises or looks ahead.
Link: a word or idea that connects two sentences (pronoun, time word, repeated noun).
Mini-chain: two or three sentences that must stay together.
Connector: words such as also, however, therefore that show how sentences relate.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A paragraph is a chain. Each sentence leaves a hook that the next one picks up. Find the hooks and the chain assembles itself.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Find the opener first. Then find sentences that begin with a reference (it, they, there, this) and attach them to the sentence they refer to. Chains first, then order the chains.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Opener test
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Coffee began as a wild plant

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Cause-effect
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Warm air rises, then moist air flows in

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Closer test
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Today it is grown in dozens of countries

mainNarrative: Look at the sentences: A "From Ethiopia the plant crossed the Red Sea…", B "Today it is grown in dozens of countries…", C "Coffee began as a wild plant in the highlands of Ethiopia", D "There, in the fifteenth century, people began roasting the beans…". Sentence C introduces coffee and has no back-reference, so it is the opener. "Today" in B marks the closer. "There" in D needs a place (Yemen) so D follows the sentence ending in Yemen.

Pronoun cues work in both directions. "its red berries" needs an earlier mention of the plant. "Through Arab scholars this system reached Europe" needs an earlier mention of a system. "This yearly cycle" in the monsoon paragraph needs the cycle to have been described, so it must come after the winter reversal.

Chronology orders histories: early number systems, then Indian mathematicians, then Arab scholars, then Europe. Cause-effect orders explanations: land heats, warm air rises, moist air flows in, rain falls.
Process of elimination helps when two sentences compete. If options differ only in the order of sentences 3 and 4, test which one the sentence 5 depends on.
Finally, read the chosen order from start to end. If you hear a jump, you have a pair out of order.

deepDiveAspects.title: A/The test
deepDiveAspects.content: A noun first mentioned takes "a"; later mentions take "the". The sentence with "the" comes after the one with "a".

deepDiveAspects.title: Connector words
deepDiveAspects.content: "Also", "further" and "a step further" show a sentence adds to an earlier point; they cannot be first.

solvedExamples.title: Opener
solvedExamples.question: Which is the opener: (A) "From Ethiopia the plant crossed the Red Sea and was first cultivated in Yemen", (B) "Coffee began as a wild plant in the highlands of Ethiopia"?

solvedExamples.title: Pronoun link
solvedExamples.question: Which sentence must come right after "There, in the fifteenth century, people began roasting the beans": "From Ethiopia the plant crossed to Yemen" or "The drink soon spread through the Arab world"?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The drink soon spread through the Arab world

solvedExamples.title: Closer
solvedExamples.question: Which is the closer: "Today it is grown in dozens of countries" or "According to legend, a goatherd noticed…"?

steps.title: Today
steps.explanation: Brings the story to the present.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Today it is grown in dozens of countries
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: "Today" marks the end of a history.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Find the opener and closer, link pronouns to their nouns, join cause-effect and time pairs, then order the chains.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting with a sentence that has "the" or a pronoun

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Also and however need something before them.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Use the first two sentences to eliminate options.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Find the closer next; it removes more options.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Each paragraph has one natural chain; the right option is the one that preserves it.
